Interface ChaosActivationHandle

All Superinterfaces:
AutoCloseable
All Known Implementing Classes:
DefaultChaosActivationHandle
public interface ChaosActivationHandle extends AutoCloseable
Live control handle for an activated chaos scenario.

Returned by ChaosControlPlane.activate(ChaosScenario) and ChaosControlPlane.activate(ChaosPlan). Implements AutoCloseable for safe use in try-with-resources blocks, which guarantees the scenario is stopped even if the test throws.

Lifecycle state machine: 

REGISTERED ── start() ──→ ACTIVE      (AUTOMATIC: inside activate(); MANUAL: handle.start())
REGISTERED ── stop() / close() ──→ STOPPED
ACTIVE ── expiry ──→ INACTIVE          (activeFor / activeUntil passed, maxApplications spent,
                                        or the stressor ended)
ACTIVE ── stop() / close() ──→ STOPPED
INACTIVE ── stop() / close() ──→ STOPPED

Only a REGISTERED scenario starts: INACTIVE and STOPPED are final for the handle, and start() on them does nothing. close() also unregisters the scenario; activating its id again registers a new one that replaces a STOPPED or INACTIVE scenario.

Once STOPPED, the handle cannot be restarted. Create a new activation to re-inject the same scenario.

Thread safety: all methods are thread-safe and can be called from any thread.

  • Method Details

    • id

      String id()
      Returns the registry key of this activation: jvm::<scenarioId> for a JVM scenario, session:<sessionId>::<scenarioId> for a session scenario, plan:<planName> for a plan. The scenario's own id is ChaosScenario.id().
      Returns:
      the activation key; never null

    • start

      void start()
      Transitions the scenario from REGISTERED to ACTIVE. For scenarios with ActivationPolicy.StartMode.AUTOMATIC, this is a no-op as they start immediately on activation.

      For stressor effects (heap pressure, deadlock, etc.), this also spawns the stressor background task. Of concurrent calls, one starts the scenario; the others return at once, possibly before it is ACTIVE.

    • stop

      void stop()
      Transitions the scenario to STOPPED, halting all effect applications. Cleans up stressor resources (background threads, retained memory, JFR periodic hooks).

      After stop(), no further effect applications will occur even if the selector still matches operations.

    • release

      void release()
      Opens a blocked ChaosEffect.GateEffect gate, releasing all threads currently blocked by this scenario without stopping the scenario itself.

      On an active scenario the gate closes again at once, so later calls are held until the next release. On an inactive scenario (its maxApplications spent, or expired) the gate opens once and is not closed again. A spent maxApplications keeps its last admitted caller at the gate until release() or stop(); expiry releases waiting threads by itself.

      Calling release() on a scenario that does not use ChaosEffect.GateEffect is a no-op. Calling it on a stopped scenario is also a no-op.

      Useful in test code to unblock operations after assertions: 

      handle.release(); // unblock the service call that was waiting on the gate
assertThat(response).isNotNull();

    • state

      ChaosDiagnostics.ScenarioState state()
      Returns the current lifecycle state of the scenario. The returned value is a snapshot; the actual state may change concurrently.
      Returns:
      the current scenario lifecycle state

    • matchedCount

      long matchedCount()

      Returns:

    • appliedCount

      long appliedCount()
      Returns how many times the scenario's effect took effect so far: the appliedCount of the diagnostics. For a plan handle, the sum over its scenarios.
      Returns:
      the application count

    • close

      default void close()
      Delegates to stop(). Enables use in try-with-resources. 
      try (ChaosActivationHandle handle = controlPlane.activate(scenario)) {
    // chaos is active here
}
// handle is stopped; stressors and gates are cleaned up
